Newborn Care

Gripe water for babies: safety, evidence and other ways to soothe

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Long periods of crying can leave you tired and ready to try almost anything that might help. Gripe water is often suggested by relatives or other parents for gas and tummy discomfort. Before giving it, ask your baby’s clinician about the crying and the exact product: a familiar remedy is not automatically effective or harmless.

Crying does not always mean trapped gas

Crying is one of a young baby’s main ways to communicate. Hunger, a wet nappy, tiredness, a need for closeness or discomfort can all be involved. As you learn your baby’s patterns, you may recognize some needs more easily, but you do not have to identify every cause on your own.

Colic describes repeated prolonged crying in an otherwise healthy baby, with no clear explanation. It often begins in the early weeks and improves by about 3 to 4 months. A baby may look tense, draw up their legs or pass wind, but those signs do not prove that gas is the main cause.

A well-fed baby can still cry for a long time. That does not establish teething, food allergy or a digestive illness either. A change from the usual cry, poor feeding or other signs of illness deserves assessment rather than another remedy.

What is in gripe water?

Gripe water is a name used for several liquid products sold for infant fussiness and digestive discomfort. It is not one standardized medicine with the same recipe in every bottle. Brands and formulations can differ between countries and can change over time.

Herbs listed in some formulations include fennel, ginger, chamomile, liquorice, cinnamon and lemon balm. Other products contain sodium bicarbonate, flavourings or sweeteners. These are examples of possible ingredients, not a recipe to make at home or a statement that every brand contains all of them.

Read both the active-ingredient and other-ingredient lists. Keep the packaging so a clinician or pharmacist can identify exactly what has been given. The word “herbal” does not tell you the concentration, purity or suitability for your baby.

Does it relieve colic, hiccups or teething?

The proposed explanation is that certain ingredients help digestion or the passage of gas. However, effects seen in adults or older children cannot simply be assumed in newborns. Nor does that explanation account for every cause of prolonged crying.

Research has not established gripe water as an effective routine treatment for infant colic. A parent may notice that a baby settles after a dose, but crying also fluctuates and babies receive feeding, cuddling and other comfort at the same time. An improvement after a product does not, by itself, show what caused it.

Products are also sometimes used for hiccups or teething discomfort. The references checked for this article do not establish benefit for those uses. A pleasant taste or a baby accepting the liquid readily is not evidence that it is needed or treating the problem.

Ingredient claims deserve a closer look

Sodium bicarbonate is baking soda, which neutralizes acid. Most infant gas is not simply an excess-acid problem, so this is not a reason to give it for colic. Do not add baking soda to a feed or use it as a homemade remedy; discuss any product containing it with a clinician.

Peppermint is another ingredient that warrants care. Oral peppermint oil can cause heartburn in some people, and infant benefit has not been established. This does not quantify the reflux risk of every gripe-water preparation. Concentrated peppermint oil or menthol should not be applied to an infant’s face or used for them to inhale.

Lists that focus only on avoiding gluten, parabens or vegetable charcoal do not establish that the remaining product is safe. A known allergy needs specific ingredient checking, while additives require assessment in the context of the whole formulation. Do not give activated charcoal as a home treatment for crying.

Avoid alcohol-containing remedies. Do not give a baby under 12 months honey or a honey-containing preparation because of the risk of infant botulism. Being sugar-free, alcohol-free or naturally flavoured still does not demonstrate effectiveness.

“For babies” is not a safety guarantee

A product marketed for babies should not be treated as proof of safety for every infant. Manufacturing quality and accurate labelling matter as well as the ingredients. There have been product-specific recalls, including a 2019 recall associated with an undissolved ingredient and reported swallowing difficulty.

Regulation differs by country and product classification. In the United States, dietary supplements are regulated, but the FDA does not approve them for safety and effectiveness before sale in the way it approves drugs. It would be inaccurate to describe this as no regulation at all.

Ask a pharmacist about the exact product, its current local status, storage and expiry. A historical recall does not mean every current brand is recalled; equally, absence of a recall is not proof that a product relieves colic.

Age, dose and timing need individual advice

There is no universal birthday after which all gripe water becomes safe or advisable. In particular, saying “not before one month” should not imply automatic approval at one month. Newborn crying deserves careful attention, and age restrictions vary with the formulation.

This article does not give a standard dose or recommend routinely giving gripe water after every feed. The claim that an immediate post-feed dose prevents gas accumulation is not established. Speak to the baby’s clinician before starting an optional remedy.

If a clinician recommends a particular licensed product for a specific reason, clarify the exact name, concentration, amount, frequency and duration, and follow those instructions and its age restrictions. Do not borrow another family’s dose, combine similar products or increase the amount because crying continues.

Possible reactions and what to do

Stop giving the product and seek advice if a new rash, itching, red watery eyes or vomiting follows it. These symptoms can have more than one cause, so record when they started and keep the bottle or a photograph of its label.

Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, breathing or swallowing difficulty, or a baby becoming floppy or difficult to wake requires emergency help. Do not wait to see whether a suspected reaction settles, and do not give another dose as a test.

A previous dose without a reaction does not guarantee future tolerance. Tell the clinician about other medicines and supplements too, rather than assuming a herbal liquid cannot interact with them.

Before changing milk or your own diet

A feeding review may be more useful than repeatedly adding remedies. Someone experienced in infant feeding can observe attachment or bottle technique, pace and the baby’s cues. For bottle feeds, support the baby semi-upright, allow pauses and avoid pushing them to finish.

An “anti-colic” bottle is not a guaranteed solution. NHS guidance does not identify one bottle or teat design as superior overall. Ease of cleaning, suitable flow and the way your baby feeds are useful things to discuss before buying more equipment.

Do not routinely remove peanuts, dairy, soya, fish and wheat from a breastfeeding parent’s diet just because a baby is unsettled. If symptoms suggest an allergy, a clinician can guide a targeted trial and nutritional support instead of a broad, indefinite restriction.

Likewise, soya formula is not a general treatment for colic. UK guidance limits its use to babies from 6 months under medical supervision; local advice may differ. Confirmed cows’ milk protein allergy may require an appropriate extensively hydrolysed or other specialist formula. Ordinary plant drinks are not an infant-formula replacement.

Other ways to comfort your baby

Try one gentle approach at a time: a cuddle, quiet talking, slow rocking or a warm bath may help. Burping during a natural pause or after a feed can be useful for some babies. Gentle touch or tummy massage while the baby is awake can be comforting, but stop if they seem uncomfortable; pressure is not a proven cure.

No settling method works every time. Note what you tried and what happened without turning each feed into a series of experiments. Ask a trusted person to take a turn if you are exhausted.

If frustration is rising, place the baby safely on their back in an empty cot and step away briefly while you get support. Never shake a baby. Needing a break is a reason to ask for help, not a sign that you have failed.

When crying needs medical help

Arrange a clinical review if the crying persists, worsens, makes feeding difficult, or is accompanied by poor growth. You can also ask for help simply because you are worried or struggling to cope; you do not need to try several products first.

Get immediate medical help for a baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher, breathing difficulty, unusual drowsiness, a weak or high-pitched cry, or other signs that something is seriously wrong. Poor feeding and markedly fewer wet nappies also need prompt assessment. Use your local urgent or emergency service rather than waiting for a colic remedy to work.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Gripe-water formulations vary, and routine benefit for infant colic has not been established.

Careful feeding assessment and support are preferable to unsupervised formula changes or broad maternal food exclusions.

Natural ingredients and infant marketing do not remove the possibility of adverse reactions or product-quality problems.

How BeMama can help

Bring the bottle or its label to a feeding or paediatric appointment and describe the crying pattern, feeding and wet nappies. This gives the discussion a clearer starting point than the product name alone.

When to seek help

Do not delay medical assessment for unusual crying, fever in a young infant, poor feeding or an allergic reaction. Breathing difficulty, significant swelling or reduced responsiveness needs emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Gripe water is a range of products, not one standardized treatment.
  • Neither a one-month age threshold nor an infant label guarantees safety.
  • Do not make routine formula or breastfeeding-diet changes without a reason and a plan.
  • Support for you matters alongside comfort and assessment for your baby.

Frequently asked questions

What does gripe water contain?

Ingredients vary. Some contain herbs such as fennel, ginger or chamomile; others include sodium bicarbonate, flavourings or sweeteners. Check the exact bottle rather than relying on a general ingredient list.

At what age can I give it?

There is no universal age that makes every formulation safe or useful. Ask your baby’s clinician before giving it and follow any product-specific restrictions; turning one month old is not automatic clearance.

Should I give it immediately after a feed?

Routine post-feed dosing to prevent trapped gas is not supported here. If a clinician recommends a particular product, ask for precise instructions rather than following a generic internet schedule.

What side effects should I watch for?

A rash, itching, watery red eyes or vomiting warrants stopping the product and seeking advice. Swelling with breathing or swallowing difficulty, or reduced responsiveness, needs emergency help.

Does it work for every colicky baby?

No. Benefit has not been established as a routine colic treatment. A baby settling after one dose cannot show whether the product, other soothing or natural variation caused the change.

Should I switch to soya formula?

Do not switch solely because of crying. A clinician can assess feeding and possible allergy, then advise whether a different formula is appropriate.

Should I cut several foods out while breastfeeding?

Routine broad exclusions are not recommended for ordinary colic. If allergy is suspected, ask for a targeted plan and nutritional support.

Can an anti-colic bottle solve the problem?

No bottle design guarantees relief. Feeding position, pace, flow and your baby’s cues are worth reviewing with a feeding professional.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
